statement: How many six-digit numbers that use each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 exactly once are divisible by 12?

choices.misconception: I only checked that the number is even, so I counted every arrangement ending in 2, 4 or 6.
I thought the last two digits had to form a multiple of 12, so I only used the endings 12, 24 and 36.
I checked only divisibility by 3, which every arrangement passes, so I counted all the arrangements.
I thought a number is divisible by 4 when its last digit is 4, so I counted the arrangements ending in 4.

hints: Split 12 into two divisibility tests that are easier to check.
A number is divisible by 12 exactly when it is divisible by 3 and by 4. See what the digit sum tells you, then count the possible last two digits.
The digit sum is 21, so divisibility by 3 is automatic. List the two-digit endings made of different digits from 1 to 6 that are multiples of 4.

solutions.reliable: Since $12 = 3 \times 4$ and 3 and 4 share no factor, the number must be divisible by 3 and by 4. The digit sum is $1 + 2 + \dots + 6 = 21$, so every arrangement is divisible by 3. For 4, the last two digits must form a multiple of 4 using two different digits from 1 to 6: 12, 16, 24, 32, 36, 52, 56, 64, which is 8 endings. The other four digits can go in front in $4! = 24$ ways, so there are $8 \times 24 = 192$ numbers. The transferable idea: test divisibility by a composite number through factors that share nothing and have simple rules.

whyOnTest: Divisibility by 12 needs two rules at once, for 3 and for 4; this probes whether you pick the right pair and apply the last-two-digits rule fully.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
